analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for oil spill cleanup costs, making big polluters pay instead of taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a vote and without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop oil companies from deducting the costs of cleaning up large oil spills (over 36,000 gallons) from their federal taxes, and would stop them from using other business losses to shield that income. Cleanup, damage, fines, and even the value of the oil lost would become taxable costs. In exchange, it lets companies immediately deduct spending on equipment and upgrades certified by the EPA as reducing the risk of a spill.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who currently absorb the revenue loss when oil companies write off spill cleanup costs as ordinary business expenses. Coastal and riverside communities also gain indirectly, because a company that cannot deduct cleanup costs, damage payments, and fines has a stronger financial reason to prevent spills in the first place.

how_it_helps.text: Companies responsible for spills of 36,000 gallons or more could no longer deduct cleanup costs, pollution-mitigation costs, damage liabilities, or the value of the lost oil, so the tax burden of a major spill would fall on the polluter rather than on federal taxpayers [S2] [S3].
The bill blocks companies from using net operating losses to offset income in the year of a spill, so a profitable-but-loss-heavy company could not escape the tax hit [S2] [S3].

It leaves small spills (under 36,000 gallons, aggregated over six months), fully cleaned-up and closed facilities, and discharges where the company is found not liable under the Oil Pollution Act or Clean Water Act deductible, aiming the penalty at major spills and at companies actually responsible for them [S3].
Section 2 lets companies immediately deduct EPA-certified spill-prevention spending instead of spreading it over years, rewarding prevention with a faster tax break [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies that cause or are liable for large spills, which would pay tax on cleanup and damage costs they currently write off. Some of that cost could trickle to consumers in slightly higher fuel prices, though the bill's prevention-expensing break partly offsets the industry's cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies liable for large spills

drawbacks.text: Because big-spill cleanup costs would come out of after-tax dollars, companies might have less cash on hand during a disaster and could skimp on cleanup speed or thoroughness — the opposite of the bill's environmental goal [S3].

The bill counts fines and penalties among the nondeductible costs, doubling a punishment that tax law already treats as nondeductible, and it makes insurance payouts for cleanup taxable income while denying the matching deduction, which some would call double taxation [S3].

The 36,000-gallon threshold (roughly a tanker truck's worth, aggregated over six months) is a bright line that ignores spill severity per gallon and would require EPA certification processes that add paperwork and delay for both companies and the agency [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that taxpayers should not subsidize the tax write-offs of companies that cause major oil spills — is sound and targeted: small spills and non-liable parties stay deductible, and prevention spending gets a faster tax break. The real drawbacks are practical: after-tax cleanup costs could slow or thin out response efforts during a disaster, and the added EPA certification and liability-determination machinery would be slow and contentious. On balance a modest, defensible measure whose main failure was political neglect rather than bad design.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Leslie Byrne introduced the bill on October 7, 1993 [S1] [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which holds jurisdiction over tax law [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and there is no further action of any kind before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies remain able to deduct major oil spill cleanup and damage costs from their taxes, and federal taxpayers continue to absorb that revenue loss.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies keeping their cleanup tax write-offs

for.name: Leslie Byrne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no colleague joined her.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat during the 103rd Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote, no report — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split was ever recorded; the bill simply sat in a Democratically controlled committee until the Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill would take away their deduction for large-spill cleanup costs, damage liabilities, and lost oil, forcing them to bear those costs in after-tax dollars; the prevention-expensing break in Section 2 is a partial offset. Today, the public effectively shares the cost of their spills through foregone tax revenue.
